items.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: But on the other hand, then there are people like, well Gerry Mulligan, for example, or Chet Baker, who use far less notes and play slightly different tone color. And in a certain way they’re making solos not from the more technical vocabulary than Parker and Gillespie and Bud Powell evolved in the

ctx.x: Yeah. Okay. Yeah. Okay. So anyway, we speak the American English language and if we hear somebody speaking that language with an accent, if we’re a student of the language if we really know it well we can identify the accent. Like in jazz there might be more of a blues accent sometimes. There might be more of a so-called cool accent in other players. There might be some players that in the course of their phrases they’re constantly changing from reaching many different levels of volume, from the softest notes in…

sometimes played a lot of notes, but when you really painstakingly learn one of the Parker solos, you can hear that every one of those notes make sense, and that one phrase really has something to do with the phrase before or with the phrase that’s coming afterwards. And very often the key notes in those phrases, the top note or the longest note, may even be the note that happens to be there in the original melody. But you have to get to more than just a completely superficial understanding of music before you…
